headline: Guatemala: From Maya Empire to Modern Nation
tldr: A 12-minute sweep through Guatemala's Maya golden age, colonial conquest, civil war, and the culture that survived it all.
summary: Guatemala sits in Central America between Mexico, Belize, Honduras, and El Salvador, split into four regions: the Pacific coastal plain holding Guatemala City, the volcano-studded northern highlands, the rainforest-covered Petén with its Maya ruins, and the eastern highlands around Lake Izabal. Three mountain chains cross the country, and its tropical climate ranges from hot lowlands to cool highlands with a May-to-October wet season prone to tropical storms. Lake Izabal is the largest lake, Lake Atitlán the scenic crater-lake draw, and the Motagua River the longest, forming part of the Honduran border.

The Maya civilization began developing around 2,000 BC and peaked in the classic period from 250 to 900 AD, building city-states like Tikal, El Mirador, and Kaminaljuyú with stone pyramids, palaces, and ball courts. They created a hieroglyphic writing system that produced texts like the Popol Vuh, and advanced mathematics, astronomy, and calendar systems, including using the concept of zero. Southern Maya cities declined around 900 AD, but northern Maya civilization carried on into the post-classic period until the Spanish arrived.

The Spanish conquered the Maya in the early 1500s, destroying texts and imposing Christianity despite scattered uprisings. Guatemala won independence in 1821, passed briefly through the Mexican Empire and a Central American federation, and became fully independent in 1839. Dictators tied to the United Fruit Company ruled from the late 1800s to 1944, a democratic government held power from 1945 to 1954 until a US-backed coup, and the resulting 36-year civil war—during which the military targeted indigenous Maya—finally ended in 1996.

Today indigenous Maya make up 40 to 60 percent of Guatemalans, led by the K'iche' along with Kaqchikel, Mam, and Q'eqchi' groups, alongside a mestizo majority and small European, African, Asian, and Middle Eastern communities. Catholicism claims 50 to 60 percent of the population, often blended with indigenous spirituality, while about 40 percent are Protestant. Spanish is official, but over 20 Mayan languages are spoken and 23 indigenous languages are officially recognized.

Guatemala's roughly $95 billion economy leans on agriculture, ranking among the world's top exporters of coffee and bananas, alongside manufacturing and tourism built around Maya sites. Despite a middle-income GDP per capita of about $8,200, over half the population lives in poverty and the US remains its top trading partner. Culturally, the country carries that mixed heritage forward through the Popol Vuh, Nobel laureate Miguel Ángel Asturias, marimba music, vivid weaving, and dishes like tamales, pepián, and jocón.
mindmap:
# Guatemala

## Geography
- Central America, borders Mexico, Belize, Honduras, El Salvador
- Four regions
  - Pacific coastal plain, Guatemala City
  - Northern highlands, volcanoes and mountains
  - Petén, lowland rainforest, Maya sites
  - Eastern highlands, Lake Izabal
- Three mountain chains
  - Sierra Madre along Pacific coast
  - Cuchumatanes and Chacas ranges
- Tropical climate varies by elevation
  - Wet season May to October
- Lakes and rivers
  - Lake Izabal, largest, 565 km²
  - Lake Atitlán, crater lake, tourist draw
  - Motagua River, longest, Honduras border

## Ancient Maya Civilization
- Settlements date to Archaic period
- Civilization develops from 2,000 BC
- Classic period peak, 250-900 AD
  - City-states: Tikal, El Mirador, Kaminaljuyú
  - Step pyramids, palaces, temples, ball courts
- Hieroglyphic writing system
  - Popol Vuh creation story
- Advances in math, astronomy, calendars
  - Concept of zero
- Southern lowlands decline around 900 AD
  - Northern Maya thrive into post-classic period

## Spanish Conquest and Colonial Rule
- Spanish arrive and conquer, early 1500s
- Captaincy General of Guatemala
- Maya texts destroyed, forced conversion
- Scattered Maya uprisings against Spanish rule

## Independence and 20th Century Turmoil
- Independence in 1821
- Briefly Mexican Empire, then Central American federation
- Fully independent in 1839
- Dictators allied with United Fruit Co
  - Late 19th century to 1944
- Democratic government, 1945-1954
- US-backed coup sparks 36-year civil war
- Civil war ends in 1996

## People and Religion
- Indigenous Maya, 40-60% of population
  - K'iche', Kaqchikel, Mam, Q'eqchi'
- Mestizo population, about 40%
- Small European, African, Asian, Middle Eastern communities
- Roman Catholicism, 50-60% of population
  - Blended with indigenous spiritual beliefs
- Protestant, about 40%
- Indigenous Maya religions still practiced

## Language
- Spanish, official language
- Over 20 Mayan languages spoken
  - K'iche', Kaqchikel, Q'eqchi', Mam main ones
- 23 indigenous languages officially recognized

## Economy
- GDP around $95 billion
- Agricultural economy
  - Top exporter of coffee and bananas
  - Corn, beans, cardamom, vegetables
- Manufacturing: food processing, textiles, pharmaceuticals
- Tourism built on nature and Maya sites
- GDP per capita around $8,200
  - Over 50% below poverty line
- United States is top trading partner

## Culture and Cuisine
- Literature
  - Popol Vuh, prehispanic hieroglyphics
  - Miguel Ángel Asturias, Nobel Prize winner
  - Luis Cardoza y Aragón, surrealism and Maya myths
- Art
  - Painting, weaving, wood carving, pottery
  - Andrés Curruchich, painter of Maya life
- Music
  - Marimba, maracas, chirimía, flutes, drums
- Cuisine
  - Corn, beans, chili, rice staples
  - Tostadas, tamales, pepián, jocón

stickies.text: This is Guatemala, once the heartland of the ancient Mayan civilization.
The Maya civilization began around 2,000 BC and peaked between 250 and 900 AD.
Mayan mathematics utilized the concept of zero and large numbers.
From the late 1800s to 1944, dictators closely allied to the United Fruit Company ruled Guatemala.
A US-backed coup in 1954 began 36 years of civil war, and indigenous Mayans were targeted by the military.
Indigenous Mayans make up about 40 to 60 percent of Guatemala's population.
Over 50 percent of the population lives below the poverty line.
Jocón, the iconic meat stew, gets its name from the Mayan word for sauce.

receipts.title: Lake Izabal is Guatemala's largest lake
receipts.detail: It covers over 565 square kilometers and, with its river tributaries, supplies water for irrigation and hydroelectric power.

receipts.title: The Motagua River forms part of the Honduras border
receipts.detail: As Guatemala's longest river, it matters both as a geographic boundary and a resource for the surrounding regions.

receipts.title: Maya mathematics used the concept of zero
receipts.detail: This advanced numerical system underpinned the astronomy and calendar work that defined classic-period Maya science.

receipts.title: Indigenous Maya remain 40-60% of the population
receipts.detail: The K'iche' are the largest group, followed by Kaqchikel, Mam, and Q'eqchi', each with its own language and traditions.

receipts.title: Over 20 Mayan languages are still spoken
receipts.detail: Spanish is official, but the government formally recognizes 23 indigenous languages alongside it.

receipts.title: GDP sits around $95 billion
receipts.detail: Guatemala is one of the world's largest exporters of both coffee and bananas, per World Bank estimates.

receipts.title: GDP per capita is about $8,200
receipts.detail: Despite middle-income status, over 50% of the population lives below the poverty line and inequality remains high.

receipts.title: The US drives over a third of Guatemala's exports
receipts.detail: It's Guatemala's top trading partner, taking over a third of exports and supplying a quarter of imports.

receipts.title: Miguel Ángel Asturias won the Nobel Prize in Literature
receipts.detail: A 20th-century Guatemalan author, he stands alongside Luis Cardoza y Aragón as a major literary figure blending Maya myth into modern writing.

events.detail: The ancient Maya began around 2,000 BC and reached their peak during the classic period, 250 to 900 AD.

events.label: Maya build great stone city-states
events.detail: Cities like Tikal, El Mirador, and Kaminaljuyú rose with step pyramids, palaces, temples, and ball courts.

events.label: Maya develop writing and the Popol Vuh
events.detail: A complex hieroglyphic writing system produced texts including the creation story Popol Vuh.

events.label: Southern Maya cities decline
events.detail: Southern lowland cities fell into decline around 900 AD, though northern Maya civilization carried on into the post-classic period.
